title: The Sleeping Smile
premise: When Elodie Winterbourne's twin brother Odile dies, they return to Winterbourne Hall to bury him — only to learn the body in the casket is Odile's, but the man who died was someone else entirely, wearing his face. Five years of rationalizing the house's noises collapse when an excavation crew unearths a door beneath the east lawn, sealed from the inside, and the crew is pulled through into a founder-era ritual chamber that is still, somehow, occupied. Elodie discovers the Winterbourne fortune was built on a pact: a twin is fed to the house each generation to keep the founders' hunger asleep, and the wrong sibling was taken this time — the house took Odile because Elodie was meant to be given. To close the door and free the trapped crew, Elodie must complete the ritual themselves, choosing whether to become the house's next keeper, destroy the pact and lose their own identity to the hunger, or pass the burden to the last living founder's descendant. Elodie chooses destruction, unmaking their name and memories in the process, and walks out of the hall as a stranger who no longer remembers why the house behind them is finally, mercifully silent.
about_author: Jonah Oyelaran is a Nigerian-British writer of quiet horror whose work explores what families bury to survive. A former archivist, he lives in a converted chapel in Yorkshire and insists the drafts under the floorboards are nothing to worry about.

chapters.title: The Wrong Body
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie returns to Winterbourne Hall for Odile's funeral and is unsettled by the open casket: the face is Odile's, but the hands are calloused wrong, and the smile in death is one Odile never wore. Aunt Vesper insists everything is fine. The beat is dread disguised as grief — the reader learns the funeral is a lie before Elodie can admit it.

chapters.title: Five Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, with a flashback structure. Elodie has stayed at the hall since the funeral, cataloguing every noise — footsteps above empty rooms, Odile's laugh in the walls — with rational explanations written in a ledger. The ledger's final entry is blank. The beat is the erosion of denial: the explanations are getting shorter, and Elodie knows it.

chapters.title: What the Ground Gives Back
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. A survey crew excavating the east lawn for drainage strikes a stone door sealed from the inside, its hinges fused. That night, the crew's foreman knocks on the hall door, soaked and mute, and Elodie realizes the other four workers never came up. The beat is the moment denial dies — the house has been waiting to be opened.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Founders
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, alternating with entries from ancestor Marguerite Winterbourne's 1843 journal. Elodie finds the founder's ledger in the sealed library: a pact, a tithe, a twin given every generation. Marguerite's last entry reads 'It smiled at me with my sister's face.' The beat is horrified recognition — Elodie was the intended offering.

chapters.title: Aunt Vesper's Bargain
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Vesper, the last living keeper, confesses she substituted Odile for Elodie five years ago, believing love would satisfy the house. She reveals the door must be closed from within by a Winterbourne before the hunger wakes fully. The beat is complicity exposed: the family's protector is its chief collaborator, and her guilt curdles into desperation.

chapters.title: The Ones Who Went Down
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie descends through the door to find the four missing crew members alive but changed — smiling, serene, slowly forgetting their names as the house wears their faces in the walls above. One begs Elodie to remember her name for her. The beat is terror tempered by tenderness; the horror has hostages, not monsters.

chapters.title: What Odile Knew
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, intercut with recovered memories. Elodie realizes the 'wrong' body was real: Odile went below willingly years ago to buy time, and what died in the casket was the house wearing him, sent up to lure Elodie down. The beat is devastating clarity — the twin bond was the mechanism all along, and Odile's sacrifice was a message: finish it.

chapters.title: The Ritual of Keeping
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. In the chamber, the founders' hunger wakes as the crew's memories fail entirely. Elodie begins the ritual of keeping, which requires a true name freely surrendered. Vesper arrives intending to force Elodie's name from them and take the keeper's power for herself. The beat is betrayal at the threshold — power's corruption made flesh in the last family member.

chapters.title: The Unmaking
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, climax. Elodie turns the ritual inside out: instead of feeding the house a name, they feed it every Winterbourne name at once — the whole inheritance, the whole pact — letting the hunger consume its own foundation. The hall convulses; the door seals itself from the outside for the first time. The beat is triumphant self-annihilation: Elodie wins by giving up everything that made them Elodie.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Gate
chapters.summary: The freed foreman's POV, epilogue. The crew walks out into daylight; the mute foreman speaks her own name aloud and it stays hers. At the gate stands a person with Elodie's face who doesn't recognize the hall, the name Winterbourne, or why they're crying. The house behind them is silent. The beat is bittersweet resolution — identity was the price, and silence is the only inheritance left.
